claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy has superior strain hardening relative to its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy fails later than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Higher compositional complexity in the quinary alloy produces locally heterogeneous lattice distortions.
Higher compositional complexity in the quinary alloy produces spatial variations in stacking-fault energy.
Local lattice distortions and spatial SFE variations promote an effective interplay between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
The quaternary and ternary subsets develop less atomic-scale inhomogeneity than the quinary alloy.
Reduced atomic-scale inhomogeneity in the lower-component subsets causes lower work-hardening rates and earlier failure.
The quinary alloy and the relevant equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets can all be prepared as single-phase FCC materials after identical thermomechanical processing.
Multiple principal elements and variable local chemical order create a rugged atomic-scale energy landscape.
Increasing the number of constituents from the ternary or quaternary subsets to the quinary alloy makes the atomic-scale energy landscape more rugged.
Stacking-fault energy influences whether deformation proceeds through dislocation slip, twinning, or martensitic transformation.
Synergistic activation of dislocation slip and deformation twinning increases strain hardening.
Synergistic activation of dislocation slip and deformation twinning delays damage accumulation.
Under identical tensile loading, the quinary alloy will have a higher work-hardening rate and delayed necking relative to the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Under identical tensile loading, the quinary alloy will have a better strength-ductility balance than the quaternary and ternary subsets.

contradictions.description: The boundary includes compressive deformation, but delayed necking and the proposed failure comparison are tensile-specific outcomes and cannot be evaluated directly in compression.
